For $\Omega$, race and ethnicity are linked to higher genre-based disagreement. Black respondents show $0.62$ more genre-based disagreement than White respondents (95\% CI $0.25$ to $0.98$), Hispanic respondents show $0.91$ more ($0.58$ to $1.25$), and respondents who identify with more than one race show $1.69$ more ($0.93$ to $2.46$), and all three are statistically significant after adjustment. Relative to respondents aged 18--29, those aged 50--59, 60--69, and 70 or older show $1.09$, $1.56$, and $1.27$ less genre-based disagreement, and all three are statistically significant after adjustment. The 40--49 group also shows less disagreement ($-0.57$), but this difference is not statistically significant after adjustment. Some college ($0.57$, 95\% CI $0.27$ to $0.88$)---relative to respondents with a high-school degree or less---and respondents with college-educated parents ($0.50$, $0.23$ to $0.77$) are also linked to higher genre-based disagreement, and both are statistically significant after adjustment. Upper-class respondents show $1.50$ more genre-based disagreement (95\% CI $0.66$ to $2.34$), about half a standard deviation of $\Omega$ (SD $2.9$). Gender, household income, and working-class identity are not statistically significant. Postgraduate education, the Midwest, and the South are significant only before adjustment.

The coherence aggregate is more concentrated, with the only statistically significant effects after adjustment being for Black respondents, who show $3.38$ more units of coherence-based disagreement (95\% CI $1.57$ to $5.19$), and upper-class respondents, who show $10.47$ more (95\% CI $6.31$ to $14.62$). In standardized terms, the upper-class coefficient is about three-quarters of a standard deviation of $\Gamma$ (SD $13.9$), larger than its $\Omega$ counterpart. Most of the upper-class difference is therefore cross-genre coherence rather than contradiction within particular genres. Hispanic identity ($2.38$ more units) and college-educated parents ($1.75$ more) show more coherence-based disagreement, but this is significant only before adjustment. Section~\ref{sec:coherence} examines the coherence component directly.

The aggregate results depend on two choices. With unweighted sums, Dimension 4 dominates $\Omega$, and its genre-based component has the largest variance (3.07, compared with 0.44 to 0.55 on the other dimensions). Three of the nine $\Omega$ coefficients that are significant after adjustment remain significant. They are Hispanic ethnic identity ($0.81$), ages 60--69 ($-0.79$), and upper-class subjective class identification ($1.52$). Black racial identity, more than one race, some college, college-educated parents, and the 50--59 and 70-or-older coefficients are no longer significant after adjustment. Black identity on $\Gamma$ is no longer significant after adjustment (Holm $p = .23$), while the upper-class effect on $\Gamma$ remains significant ($12.62$). On a log scale, eight of the nine adjusted-significant $\Omega$ coefficients remain significant. The upper-class coefficient is no longer significant, falling to $0.13$ (95\% CI $0.02$ to $0.23$, Holm $p = .25$).

The dimension-specific models check where the aggregate effects come from. Because OLS is linear in the outcome, each aggregate coefficient equals the sum of the dimension coefficients divided by that dimension's standard deviation, so the decomposition is exact (Tables~\ref{tab:regression}, \ref{tab:omega-regression}, and \ref{tab:coherence-regression} in Appendix~\ref{app:regression}). The upper-class coefficient on $\Omega$ comes mainly from Dimension 2 ($0.61$ in standardized units, significant after adjustment at the dimension level) and Dimension 4 ($0.43$, significant only before adjustment). Race effects come mainly from Dimension 3, which supplies $0.38$ of the Hispanic coefficient of $0.91$ and $0.26$ of the Black coefficient of $0.62$. The age decline on $\Omega$ combines declines on Dimension 1 and Dimension 3 at ages 60--69 ($-1.07$ and $-0.90$), partly offset by increases on Dimensions 2 and 4. 

Of the 96 coefficients in the dimension-level disagreement models, 12 are statistically significant after adjustment. On the highbrow--popular dimension, disagreement falls with age from 30--39 through 60--69. On volume, upper-class respondents and those with college-educated parents show more disagreement. On the engagement divide, Black respondents, respondents who identify with more than one race, those aged 60 and older, and Westerners have significant coefficients after adjustment. On status valuation, only the upper class is significant after adjustment, narrowly (Holm $p \approx .04$). In the log-outcome models, the upper-class effects on $W_2$ and $W_4$ remain significant, while the age coefficients on $W_4$ do not.

\subsection{Which Genres Anchor Complex Tastes? Demographic Concentration}
\label{sec:genre-specificity}

Section~\ref{sec:social} found that demographics account for $9.9\%$ of the variation in the genre-based aggregate $\Omega$. That result does not show where the patterning sits among the twenty genres. To answer that question, we split $\Omega$ into its genre components, $\Omega_g(i)$. For each genre $g$, we fit an OLS model of $\Omega_g(i) = \sum_{s=1}^{4} \omega_s(i;g)/\mathrm{SD}_s$, the genre's part of the aggregate on the same scale. The models use the covariates of Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression} and the same 2,258 respondents. The genre contributions sum to $\Omega$, and OLS is linear in the outcome, so the twenty coefficients for any covariate sum exactly to its coefficient in the aggregate model. Each genre coefficient is therefore that genre's part of the aggregate association, and the parts can point in different directions.

Figure~\ref{fig:genre-omega-forest} shows the fourteen covariates with at least one genre coefficient that is statistically significant after Holm adjustment across all 480 genre coefficients. Genres are ordered by their position on Dimension 3 (the engagement divide), running from reggae and rap/hip-hop at the top to heavy metal and indie rock at the bottom. Each genre's position is its mean category coordinate on that dimension across the three aspects. Filled markers indicate coefficients that are statistically significant after adjustment.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-omega-forest}
\caption{Genre-specific aggregate disagreement. Each point is the coefficient from a separate OLS model of $\Omega_g(i)$, the genre's part of the SD-weighted aggregate, on the covariates of Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression} ($N = 2{,}258$). Bars show 95\% confidence intervals. Filled markers indicate Holm-adjusted $p < .05$ across all 480 genre coefficients. Panels show only covariates with at least one coefficient that is statistically significant after adjustment. Omitted covariates are other race, income (\$25--49k, \$50--74k, \$75k+), working, middle, and upper class, and Midwest, South, and West. We omit the upper class even though its aggregate coefficient is statistically significant in Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression}, because no genre coefficient is. Genres are ordered by their position on Dimension 3, from reggae and rap/hip-hop at the top to heavy metal and indie rock at the bottom.}
\label{fig:genre-omega-forest}
\end{figure}

Age shows the clearest pattern. At ages 70 and older, indie rock ($0.60$ units less disagreement, 95\% CI $0.52$ to $0.68$ less) and rap/hip-hop ($0.58$ units less, 95\% CI $0.49$ to $0.67$ less) account for $93\%$ of the aggregate age effect of $1.27$ units less disagreement, suggesting older respondents are particularly unified in their tastes for these genres (primarily preferred by younger people). The pattern of unification around youth-oriented genres starts earlier, with rap/hip-hop ($0.29$ units less) and indie rock ($0.23$ units less) already lower at ages 40 to 49. Heavy metal and reggae show less disagreement at ages 60 and older, and dance/club does so at ages 50 to 69, with differences that are significant after adjustment. Respondents aged 70 and older show higher disagreement in big band ($0.25$), musicals ($0.17$), bluegrass ($0.13$), and gospel ($0.10$), along with several smaller increases in disagreement that are significant after adjustment.

Race and ethnicity follow a different pattern. Black respondents' aggregate difference ($0.62$ units more) is spread across eleven genres, with significant differences after adjustment in both directions. Black respondents show more genre-based disagreement in rap/hip-hop ($0.36$ units, 95\% CI $0.29$ to $0.43$), reggae ($0.32$ units, $0.24$ to $0.40$), blues/R\&B ($0.21$ units), gospel ($0.15$ units), and jazz ($0.13$ units). They show less in heavy metal ($0.22$ units less, 95\% CI $0.15$ to $0.29$), indie rock ($0.16$ units less, $0.09$ to $0.22$), controversial rock ($0.15$ units less), bluegrass ($0.13$ units less), and folk ($0.11$ units less). Here, genre-based disagreement means how far a respondent's preference, engagement, and evaluation pull apart within a genre, not disagreement between people. These genres also have the largest Black audiences. Among respondents who like each genre, the Black share is $23\%$ in rap/hip-hop, $23\%$ in gospel, $21\%$ in reggae, $19\%$ in blues/R\&B, and $16\%$ in jazz, against $12\%$ in the sample. It is $7\%$ in heavy metal, $9\%$ in indie rock, and $9\%$ in controversial rock.

The Hispanic coefficient ($0.91$) is largely driven by Latin/salsa ($0.52$ units more, $0.46$ to $0.57$), which also has the largest Hispanic-liking audience: $38\%$ of its likers are Hispanic, compared with $16\%$ of the sample. Respondents of more than one race show more disagreement in reggae ($0.43$ units, $0.26$ to $0.60$), Latin/salsa ($0.25$), and dance/club ($0.22$), all significant after adjustment. Asian respondents show less disagreement in indie rock ($0.24$ units less) and more in oldies ($0.14$ units), but their aggregate difference ($0.21$ units) is not significant after adjustment.

Education and parents' education are linked to a small number of genres. Postgraduate respondents show more disagreement in folk ($0.18$ units), opera ($0.18$), and musicals ($0.10$), all significant after adjustment. Bachelor's-educated respondents show one significant genre, folk ($0.10$ units more disagreement), and some-college respondents show one, jazz ($0.05$ units). Respondents with college-educated parents show more disagreement in opera ($0.08$ units), musicals ($0.07$), and classical music ($0.04$), all significant after adjustment. Opera and musicals recur across both education measures.

Women show lower disagreement in heavy metal ($-0.14$, 95\% CI $-0.19$ to $-0.10$) and higher disagreement in musicals ($0.06$, $0.04$ to $0.08$). Women are $45\%$ of heavy metal's likers and $58\%$ of musicals' likers, against $52\%$ of the sample. Gospel and Latin/salsa have larger female shares than musicals but no significant female coefficient after adjustment. Neither appears in the aggregate, where the gender difference is $0.07$ units less and not significant. Household income, subjective class other than upper class, and census region show no genre coefficient that is significant after adjustment. The upper-class aggregate difference ($1.50$ units) is spread across the genres, and the largest genre contribution is opera ($0.20$ units more disagreement, 95\% CI $0.09$ to $0.30$, Holm $p = .08$).

Across the twenty genres, group audience shares and group differences move together. The Black share of a genre's liking audience correlates with how much more genre-based disagreement Black respondents show than White respondents ($r = 0.88$, 95\% CI $0.72$ to $0.95$). The Hispanic share correlates with the Hispanic--White difference ($r = 0.91$, $0.78$ to $0.96$), and the female share with the woman--man difference ($r = 0.81$, $0.57$ to $0.92$). Each genre's overall liking rate is nearly unrelated to the Black share ($r = -0.02$), and controlling for it leaves the partial correlations at $0.89$, $0.91$, and $0.80$.


\subsection{The Social Patterning of Cross-Genre Coherence}
\label{sec:coherence}

The genre-based aggregate $\Omega$ is socially patterned. Age, race, and education are linked to disagreement in particular genres (Section~\ref{sec:genre-specificity}), and upper-class identity shows no genre-level coefficient that is statistically significant after adjustment. But what about the coherence component---the reinforcing or canceling of per-genre disagreements across the full repertoire? 

We tested this with the same demographic variables and methods. Demographics explain $3.9\%$ of the variation in the coherence aggregate $\Gamma$, against $9.9\%$ for $\Omega$ (Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression}), and only the Black and upper-class coefficients are statistically significant after adjustment. The dimension-level coherence models (Table~\ref{tab:coherence-regression}) serve as the robustness check. Of their 96 coefficients, 17 reach $p < .05$ unadjusted, and 6 are statistically significant after adjustment. These six are Black respondents on $\gamma_3$, ages 40--49 and 50--59 on $\gamma_1$, college-educated parents on $\gamma_2$, and upper-class identity on $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_4$. Gender shows no significant coefficient on any dimension, and household income shows none after adjustment.

Because $\Omega_i + \Gamma_i$ is the SD-scaled sum of $W_s(i)$, the split in Equation~\ref{eq:genre} carries over to the aggregate coefficients. The upper-class coefficient on the total is $11.97$, the sum of $1.50$ on $\Omega$ and $10.47$ on $\Gamma$, so about 87\% of the upper-class difference is coherence. The same total can arise from one genre held in intense contradiction or from many genres tilted the same way, and social position is associated with which form prevails.

Coherence is not always reinforcing. A considerable share of respondents show negative coherence, meaning their per-genre disagreements partially cancel and their total disagreement is smaller than the sum of its genre-level parts. About a third on the highbrow--popular dimension ($33\%$), a quarter on the volume dimension ($25\%$), and more than half on the engagement-divide dimension ($52\%$). One caveat concerns the status-valuation dimension. Evaluation is the only aspect that varies there, so a respondent who grants high status to many genres displaces their evaluation point in the same direction for every genre at once. For such respondents, much of what $\gamma_4$ records is this uniform displacement rather than configural contradiction, which is why $\gamma_4$ correlates with the magnitude of the global position ($r = 0.79$). Where coherence has social structure, then, it reflects these repertoire-wide orientations rather than localized contradiction. The genre-anchored form of complex taste---the kind whose social geography the previous section mapped---is the genre-based component's contribution.

\subsection{Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure. We've traced them from the individual perspective, asking \emph{who} has complex tastes and \emph{what} aspects disagree. But genres are targets too. Which genres attract complex tastes? The answer is that some genres generate much simpler responses than others.\footnote{At the genre level, we measure the proportion of respondents with simple tastes. These are the respondents whose three aspects all agree (either all yes---like, listen, grant status---or all no). The complement is the proportion with complex tastes in that genre (any mismatch across aspects).}

Heavy metal, Latin/salsa, and bluegrass produce largely simple tastes. Respectively, $70\%$, $67\%$, and $65\%$ of respondents respond consistently across all three aspects. You either like them and listen and value them, or you don't. Classical and opera are different. Only $33\%$ and $24\%$ of respondents respond simply to these genres. The rest hold them in contradiction. They might like classical music but rarely listen to it, or they listen out of cultural obligation while withholding judgments about the fans, or they think the music lacks status yet listen regularly. These prestige genres splinter audiences into complex configurations.

To answer this, we need a different analysis. The first MFA treated respondents as the units being analyzed and genres as variables. Now we flip that. Rows become genres and columns become respondent-responses (each respondent's yes/no on liking, listening, and evaluation for each genre). We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This is not simply a rearrangement of the original solution; it is a different analysis that asks new questions. In the original analysis, genres appeared only as variables; we could locate them through the composition of their audiences---the average profile of people who affirm them. But we cannot compute aspect-level agreement from the respondent analysis alone. Specifically, we cannot ask whether genres that are \emph{liked by many} are also \emph{listened to by many}---that is, whether the liking and listening audiences for each genre overlap. We also cannot see whether different aspects place individual genres in different positions. Both questions require treating genres as the units of analysis and respondents as the indicators.

Technically, this flip changes the analysis. Because MFA weights each block inversely to its separate analysis's strength in the first dimension, and transposing reshuffles which variables define the blocks, the balancing weights change. The transposed separate analyses yield different first eigenvalues ($\lambda_1' = 0.153/0.161/0.419$ for preference/consumption/evaluation respondent-indicators, versus the original $0.1550/0.1265/0.1942$ for genre-indicators). The transposed dimensions are thus optimized for spreading genres apart, not respondents. The key statistics we want---RV coefficients comparing aspects at the genre level, and aspect-specific partial points showing where different respondent-groups place each genre---do not exist in the respondent-level fit.\footnote{The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level analysis. Eigenvalues, global and partial points, RV coefficients, and group contributions are numerically consistent.}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map-d12} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA (dimensions 1--2). Black points mark genre compromise positions. Colored points mark aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions). Grey leader lines connect each genre's label to its compromise point.}
\label{fig:genre-map-d12}
\end{figure}

From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} more. The RV coefficients jump to $0.92$ (preference and consumption nearly identical), $0.53$ (preference and evaluation), and $0.48$ (consumption and evaluation)---much higher than the individual-level $0.35$, $0.01$, and $0.02$. At the genre level, people who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans high status. Genres that recruit likers recruit listeners too.

This is an aggregation result rather than a contradiction of the individual-level finding. The liking audience and the listening audience overlap for each genre. But the \emph{same individuals} don't always inhabit both groups. The person who likes opera but doesn't listen is in the liking audience; the person who listens but doesn't like is in the listening audience. Separately, they agree. Together, at the aggregate genre level, they agree. But at the individual level, people split apart. Complex tastes aren't something genres do; they're something individuals experience. Which individuals respond simply and which complexly varies person by person.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Genre target profiles showing the percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space has the following eigenvalues ($\lambda_1 = 2.25$, $14.8\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.93$, $12.8\%$; $\lambda_3 = 1.25$, $8.2\%$; $\lambda_4 = 1.12$, $7.4\%$), with the first four dimensions accounting for $43.2\%$ of the total variation. The first two dimensions are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}, and the fourth dimension is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d14}. 

The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($+3.5$), opera ($+3.0$), and musicals ($+2.0$), with distant-praise rates correlating at $\rho = +0.84$ and taste-pose rates at $\rho = +0.59$---against genres most often held in the guilty pleasure ($\rho = -0.79$)\footnote{The correlation coefficients ($\rho$) reported throughout this section are Spearman rank correlations between each genre's position on the transposed dimension and the genre-level prevalence (proportion of respondents, across all 2,259) who hold that genre in each of Ma's eight configuration types. For example, $\rho = +0.84$ for distant praise on Dimension 1 means that genres with high positive values on that dimension tend to have high prevalence of distant-praise configurations, while genres with negative values tend to have low prevalence of that configuration.} and distanced consumption ($-0.82$) configurations. These last include top 40 ($-2.1$), rap/hip-hop ($-1.6$), classic rock/oldies ($-1.6$), and contemporary rock ($-1.4$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement. This dimension, in plain terms, measures the \emph{engagement--detachment} contrast at the genre level. On the positive side sit prestige genres whose audiences are defined partly by abstention from engagement (the listener who values classical music highly but rarely listens), while the negative side includes genres where respondents' disagreement arises from active engagement despite reservations about status (the guilty-pleasure listener who loves the genre but withholds attributing high status to the genre's audience). In effect, this dimension answers the question of whether a genre recruits audiences through engagement or through distant admiration.

The second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}. Genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}; Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}). At the positive pole sit the genres most often held in simple non-taste ($\rho = +0.80$)---rap/hip-hop ($+1.7$), reggae ($+1.5$), Latin/salsa ($+1.4$), and heavy metal ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = -0.81$), as taste poses ($-0.59$), as guilty pleasures ($-0.43$), or as justified abstentions ($-0.40$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($-3.5$), mood/easy listening ($-2.1$), and country ($-1.7$). Opera ($+1.0$) is a partial exception. Its characteristic configuration is distant praise (with $58.9\%$ of respondents holding it in that configuration), yet its position sits on the non-taste side, alongside a low consumption rate ($8.5\%$). The duality is asymmetric in the way complex-taste theory anticipates. The prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is among the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera, against $8.2\%$ for bluegrass).

The partial points reveal how audiences for the same genre diverge by aspect. Like in our original MFA analysis focused on individuals, in the transposed MFA, each genre has three partial points per dimension. One is for the preference-audience (respondents who like it), one for the consumption-audience (respondents who listen), and one for the evaluation-audience (respondents who grant it high status). When these three points cluster together, a genre recruits the same people across all three aspects---likers and listeners and status-granters occupy the same region. When they spread far apart, a genre's audiences are segmented. The people who like it are positioned differently from those who listen to it or who value its fans highly. The configuration axis (Dimension 2 of Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}) shows this segmentation most directly. Rap/hip-hop illustrates the pattern on the simple-non-taste pole. Its liking and listening audiences sit at $+2.8$ and $+1.9$, while its evaluation audience sits at $+0.4$. Classic rock/oldies shows the opposite arrangement, with liking and listening audiences far on the other side ($-4.8$ and $-5.5$) and status-granters near the middle ($-0.2$). Opera splits across the origin, with preference and consumption on the simple-non-taste side ($+2.2$ and $+1.4$) and evaluation on the other side ($-0.7$). In each case, the people who grant a genre high status occupy a different position on this axis from the people who like or listen to it. 

More broadly, three patterns emerge. Opera has the widest spread across its three partial points on the status-without-engagement dimension (3.1 points), where its status-granting audience sits even further toward the prestige pole ($+4.9$) than its liking and listening audiences do ($+2.5$ and $+1.8$). Classic rock/oldies has the widest spread on the configuration axis (5.3 points). Its liking and listening audiences sit at $-4.8$ and $-5.5$, while its status-granting audience sits near the middle ($-0.2$). Most other genres recruit relatively unified audiences where the same people like, listen, and evaluate, or where segmentation concentrates on a single dimension rather than cutting across multiple ways of relating to the music.

The fourth dimension orders genres by the racial composition of their audiences. Blues/R\&B ($+2.7$ and $+2.5$ for its liking and listening partial points), jazz ($+2.4$ and $+1.9$), and rap/hip-hop ($+1.1$ and $+1.8$) sit at the positive pole, and Black respondents make up $19\%$, $16\%$, and $23\%$ of their liking audiences, against $12\%$ of the sample. Gospel and reggae also sit high ($+0.7$ and $+0.5$), with Black shares of $23\%$ and $21\%$. At the negative pole sit heavy metal ($-2.5$ and $-1.7$), country ($-2.0$ and $-3.0$), indie rock, bluegrass, and folk, whose liking audiences are $6$--$9\%$ Black. Across the twenty genres, a genre's position correlates at $r = 0.75$ with the Black share of its liking audience (95\% CI $0.46$ to $0.90$), and dropping any single genre leaves the correlation between $0.73$ and $0.79$. Controlling for each genre's liking rate (the proportion of respondents who like it), the partial correlation is $0.78$ (95\% CI $0.51$ to $0.91$; permutation $p < .001$). The white share shows the mirror pattern (partial $r = -0.63$, 95\% CI $-0.84$ to $-0.25$), but the two shares are related ($r = -0.77$). In a joint model with the liking rate, the Black share is the only one of the two shares that remains significant ($b = 14.8$, SE $4.9$, $p = .008$), and the white share adds nothing once the Black share is included ($b = -0.47$, $p = .87$). The Hispanic share correlates at $0.15$ in raw terms. The female share of liking audiences correlates at $0.39$ in raw terms, but this association does not survive controls (partial $r = 0.37$ given the liking rate, 95\% CI $-0.10$ to $0.70$; partial $r = -0.18$ given the Black share).\footnote{Controlling for each genre's listening rate instead of its liking rate gives a partial correlation of $0.75$ for the Black share (95\% CI $0.44$ to $0.90$; permutation $p < .001$) and $-0.54$ for the white share (95\% CI $-0.80$ to $-0.11$; permutation $p = .014$). Rank-based partial correlations controlling for liking rate are $0.84$ for the Black share and $-0.69$ for the white share. Confidence intervals use the Fisher $z$ transformation with standard error $1/\sqrt{n-4}$, and permutation $p$-values come from 10{,}000 shuffles of the residualized audience shares.} Evaluation contributes only $7\%$ of this axis, and its partial points span roughly $\pm0.6$ against roughly $\pm3$ for liking and listening, so the dimension describes who likes and listens to genres rather than who grants them status. Mood/easy listening also has a positive position but a near-average Black liking audience ($13\%$), so race does not explain its position. The individual-level engagement divide (Dimension 3) is also racially patterned, carrying about two-fifths of the aggregate Hispanic and Black coefficients (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

Colored points mark aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions). Grey leader lines connect each genre's label to its compromise point. \section{Discussion}

The core finding is that cultural taste is not unified. We measure complex tastes as the gaps between what people prefer, what they listen to, and what they think has status. Three large aspects of musical taste emerge, surprisingly distinct from one another. Preference and consumption overlap modestly, but evaluation follows a largely different logic. Knowing whether someone likes many genres tells you little about which genres they grant high status to. This separability creates space for complexity: people can like without listening, listen without granting status, or combine the three in various ways. This structure yields four dimensions, each capturing a familiar distinction about taste: whether someone favors prestigious or popular genres; how much music they engage with overall; which musical worlds they inhabit; and how generously they distribute status attributions across genres. People's preferences and listening habits are tightly linked on the first three dimensions, while the status dimension operates mostly on its own.

This setup has implications for how we think about cultural judgment. It suggests that taste is multidimensional in a specific, interpretable way. The highbrow--popular hierarchy that researchers have documented for decades is clearly visible in liking and listening. But the willingness to grant high status to genre fans is a separate matter, unmoored from actual consumption patterns. Someone can listen to hip-hop regularly without thinking its fans merit high status, or conversely, grant high status to blues fans while never listening to blues. Bourdieu's classic account of taste as a homology between social position and cultural positions is partially borne out---the prestige hierarchy clearly stratifies by age and class---but the full picture is more complicated. Social position does structure where people sit on the highbrow--popular axis, but not as clearly whether and how much their aspects disagree.

Despite this complexity, disagreement is not primarily a signature of privilege. Complex tastes are widespread. The average respondent holds roughly half of the 20 genres in one of Ma's six complex configurations (a situation where the aspects misalign), and only 12 of 2,259 respondents hold no complex configuration at all. Yet race, age, education, and class explain only a modest share of how disagreement varies. The largest demographic associations concentrate in particular genres and their audiences---older respondents' distance from rap and indie rock, Black respondents' alignment with gospel and blues, Hispanic respondents' connection to Latin genres. This suggests that complex taste is not driven primarily by overall social position, but by engagement with specific cultural worlds. A person might be unified in their taste for classical music but split in their attitude toward hip-hop. The apparent contradiction between individual-level separation and genre-level alignment makes sense once we recognize that genre audiences are composites. A genre like opera can look coherent in aggregate---most people who like opera also listen to it and think its fans are high status---while the individuals within that audience are heterogeneous \citep{lahire2011plural-519}. Some like it without listening; others listen without granting it status. A genre's likers, listeners, and status-granters overlap, but the same individuals need not occupy all three roles.

These patterns are associations observed in a single cross-sectional survey, so they describe correlation, not causation. Omitted variables---family taste history, peer influence, identity work, exposure to different genres---could drive both disagreement and demographic associations. The cross-sectional design means we cannot track whether aspects converge or diverge as people age or change life circumstances, a question that matters for understanding taste as stable identity or as responsive practice. We also cannot verify that Dimension 3, which is racially patterned at the individual level, is the same dimension as Dimension 4, which is ordered by the racial composition of genre audiences. To address these limits, panel or repeated surveys would track aspect alignment over time. Split-sample checks and respondent-level analysis with survey weights would test whether the race and gender patterns reflect individual choices, genre history, or audience composition.

The measure of complex taste itself comes with caveats. We interpret disagreement scores geometrically, as a respondent's aspects pulling them toward different locations in the taste space, but we have no direct validation against survey items on ambivalence or guilt (the data codebook contains no such measures). The interpretation rests on the argument that a profile whose aspects place a person in different locations cannot be summarized by any single taste position, and therefore merits the label "complex." This justifies the interpretation without settling it definitively. Several coding choices shape what the disagreement scores capture. Unfamiliarity is treated as non-liking, so preference prevalence partly reflects familiarity rather than taste. 

Evaluation is a constructed binary derived from genre prestige judgments and class identity, a judgment call that could be coded differently. Dimension 2, the volume axis, draws mainly on the same liking and listening answers that define its conceptual scope, so its observed association with preference and consumption says more about the axis structure itself than about taste structure. Ma's categorical approach---which counts genres in complex configurations---offers a complementary view. The two agree modestly: disagreement as measured geometrically correlates 0.61--0.63 with configuration counts on some dimensions but barely at all on others (especially coherence, which is mostly of the cross-genre kind that Ma's framework doesn't capture). Neither measure is complete; both are useful depending on the question. To validate and extend the geometric measure, future work might use direct ambivalence and guilt items, behavioral or observational measures of evaluation (such as how respondents describe genre audiences in their own words), and alternate coding schemes to test robustness.

All of this comes from a single 2012 online survey with 20 genres and U.S. adults only. The sample is unweighted, and we treat 412 respondents (mostly those who grant high status to no genre) as supplementary because they are constant within at least one aspect block. Refitting with them as active respondents yields dimensions that correlate 0.87--0.97 with the main fit, suggesting the results are stable, but the unweighted analysis describes this sample rather than the population. A single cross-section cannot show whether complex configurations persist over time, whether aspect alignment changes across the life course, or whether the four-dimension structure holds for other genre sets or countries. The results are best understood as a measurement proposal, tested in this sample, pending verification in other samples, other cultural fields (film, fashion, visual art), and other countries.

The statistical summaries are provisional. We constructed the aggregate scores from dimension-specific scores and weighted them so each dimension contributes equally. We chose this weighting after comparing alternatives based on their correlations with configuration counts, making it exploratory. Using the unweighted sum instead, or a log transformation, changes which coefficients survive multiple-comparison correction. The outcomes are right-skewed, so the normal-approximation confidence intervals may be loose. The 20 genres are not independent units (the same respondents answer all of them), so correlations and overlapping cells introduce dependence. Respondent-level analysis and sensitivity checks in new samples would test the robustness of these findings.

Stepping back, what does all of this tell us about taste and culture? The results bear on several theoretical conversations. The debate over cultural omnivorousness has focused on consumption breadth---whether people like many genres or few. But breadth in liking and listening sits on a separate axis from breadth in status attribution. Someone can like many genres while granting status to few, or vice versa. A model that treats consumption breadth as a proxy for cultural standing would miss half the structure. Bourdieu's prediction that social structure manifests in taste space is partially supported: the highbrow--popular hierarchy is clearly stratified. But Bourdieu did not anticipate that a population with separable aspects could generate widespread disagreement that carries little social signature. This qualifies his theory: class and education structure which genres someone encounters and values overall, but not necessarily how unified their taste profile is.

The dual findings---aspects aligned at the genre level but separate at the individual level---show why unit of analysis matters. Genre-level patterns and individual-level patterns are meaningful—perhaps different questions and rest on different samples. A claim that an opera audience is coherent in its status attributions does not describe the individuals within that audience, many of whom may split their preferences, consumption, and evaluations across genres. This has methodological implications for taste research: individual taste and genre audience are different objects, and mixing levels can confound results.

Finally, the results suggest that cultural judgment is less unified than a single taste dimension would imply. The traditional prestige hierarchy is real and consequential, but it coexists with other structures and with substantial individual variation in how the three aspects align. This fragmentation may itself be socially meaningful---perhaps expressing tension between prescribed taste hierarchies and lived engagement with music, or between identity-work assertions and actual practice. Testing this would require understanding taste as performance and positioning, not just as preference. This measurement proposal offers one lens for that work. Whether the geometric measure of disagreement captures something real about cultural life, or whether other fields show the same four-dimensional structure, remains to be seen.

\section{Comparison of the Geometric and Discrete Approach}
\label{app:comparison}

\subsection{Comparing the Two Measures}
\label{sec:antinomies}

Geometric complex taste is one way to capture complex tastes, and Ma's categorical complex taste, which uses the configurations, offers another. The two mostly do not coincide. The configuration count correlates only weakly with $W_s(i)$, and the weakness comes mainly from coherence, the cross-genre part of $W_s(i)$. Ma's framework works genre by genre. It classifies a person's preference, engagement, and evaluation of each genre into one of eight configurations. Two of these have the three aspects agreeing, and six have them diverging, such as guilty pleasures, taste poses, and distanced consumption (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines them). Counting how many of a person's 20 genres fall into the six complex configurations gives their total count of complex tastes, the number of genres in which they hold one of these six configurations.

Most of $W_s(i)$ is coherence. It makes up 85--89\% of the variance in $W_s(i)$ on each dimension, and the configuration counts correlate only weakly with it (all $|\rho| \le 0.21$). The genre-based component behaves differently. The total count correlates with it at 0.61, 0.58, 0.63, and 0.24 across the four dimensions, against 0.17, 0.28, 0.18, and $-0.11$ for $W_s(i)$. Most of the disagreement lies in coherence, which correlates with the counts at 0.21 or less in absolute value, because the configurational approach classifies genres one at a time and has no cross-genre term. The total count also correlates with the global positions, at $0.66$ on the volume dimension and $-0.40$ on the highbrow--popular dimension.

Figure~\ref{fig:signatures} shows how each configuration count correlates with four geometric measures on each dimension. The four measures are the global position, the aspect-disagreement score, its genre-based component, and its coherence component. The configuration types differ in their signatures. Distant praise and taste poses correlate positively with the status-valuation global position ($\rho = 0.69$ and $0.42$), guilty pleasures correlate negatively with it ($\rho = -0.40$), and guilty pleasures correlate with the genre-based components on the highbrow--popular and engagement-divide dimensions ($\rho = 0.50$ and $0.47$). These are point estimates from Spearman correlations among $N = 2{,}259$ respondents, with no confidence intervals, so differences of a few hundredths should not be read as meaningful.

Configurations are also heterogeneous internally. Among respondents with guilty pleasures, the status-valuation score $W_4$ has a mean of $4.5$ and an SD of $10.4$, so the same configuration spans different degrees of disagreement, depending on which genres hold it and how much the aspects disagree within them.\footnote{Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} visualizes the full range of within-configuration variation across all eight configurations and four dimensions.}

Heatmap shows Spearman correlations between configuration counts (per respondent, out of 20 genres) and MFA global positions and aspect-disagreement scores ($N = 2{,}259$), across four dimensions and four score types (global positions, aspect-disagreement, its genre-based component, and its coherence component).}
\label{fig:signatures}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Within-Configuration Variation in Disagreement Scores}
\label{app:config-variation}

Respondents classified into the same configuration type show variation in their aspect-disagreement scores across all four dimensions. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} shows the mean and standard deviation of $W_s$ for each configuration, revealing that overlap in disagreement levels within and across configuration types helps explain the weak correlation between the geometric and combinatorial measures. One plausible reason is that the same configuration can span different numbers of genres and different internal structures, so respondents who share a configuration can differ in $W_s$. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} shows the variation but does not decompose it, so this explanation is a hypothesis. The disagreement associated with a particular configuration depends not just on its presence, but on how spread out it is across the genre space.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-variation} \caption{Aspect-disagreement scores by configuration type. Bars show the mean $W_s$ for each of Ma's eight configurations on each of the four dimensions; error bars show $\pm 1$ SD. The overlap both within and across configuration types is consistent with the weak correlation between configuration counts and geometric disagreement scores.}
\label{fig:config-variation}
\end{figure}

\section{The Combinatorial Measure and Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation). Two of the eight are simple, namely the simple taste $(+++)$ and the simple non-taste $(---)$, and six are complex.

Under this classification, complex configurations are the common case. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration. The average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$). Respondents often like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't think of as high status. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration. These results describe this survey and this classification, not an established population norm.

\section{Genre-Specific Disagreement Across All Twenty Genres}
\label{app:omega-genres}

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4} show the genre-by-demographic matrices for all twenty genres, one figure per dimension. Each cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable (rows) and the genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$ of the genre named in the column. All thirty demographic indicators are shown. They include the four own-education categories (high school or less, some college, bachelor's, postgraduate), parents' education, the four subjective-class identities (lower, working, middle, upper), gender, the six age groups, the six race and ethnicity categories (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, Multirace, Other), the four income categories, and the four census regions. Each indicator is a 0/1 variable; blue cells are positive, red cells negative, and every value is printed.

The matrices show which genres carry the demographic patterning. On the highbrow--popular dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}) the age gradient appears in the popular block (rap/hip-hop $0.31$, indie rock $0.25$, and dance/club $0.18$ for ages 18--29, against $-0.23$ for rap/hip-hop at ages 70+), the race indicators peak in Latin/salsa (Hispanic respondents $0.44$, White $-0.34$), and Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$) and blues ($0.23$). On the volume dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d2}) the education contrasts appear (postgraduate respondents $0.17$ for opera and $0.15$ for musicals, parents' education $0.15$ for opera and $0.12$ for classical music and musicals) alongside the race contrasts in the diaspora genres (Hispanic respondents $0.34$ for Latin/salsa, Black respondents $0.20$ for gospel and $0.18$ for reggae). On the engagement-divide dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d3}) the first dimension's age and race patterns recur at nearly full strength (rap/hip-hop $0.31$ for ages 18--29; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White). On the status-valuation dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) the associations are weak throughout; the largest is postgraduate respondents in opera ($0.18$).

\section{Genre-Specific Contributions to Configuration Positions}
\label{app:config-own}

Each configuration barycenter in Section~\ref{sec:config-cloud} averages whole respondent profiles, so it includes the contributions of the other genres. This appendix isolates the part of each position that comes from the genre itself. For genre $g$ and configuration $c$, let
$$O_{gcs} = \sum_{h=1}^{3} (z_{c,h} - p_{gh})\,\Delta_{ghs},$$
where $z_{c,h}$ is 1 if the configuration answers yes in aspect $h$ and 0 otherwise, and $p_{gh}$ and $\Delta_{ghs}$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:disagreement}. The term $O_{gcs}$ is the genre's contribution to the global position on dimension $s$ for any respondent who holds $c$ for $g$. Because it depends on the configuration alone, no averaging across respondents is involved. Summing it over the twenty genres gives each respondent's global position exactly, so $\sum_{g} O_{g,c_{ig},s} = F_s(i)$, where $c_{ig}$ is respondent $i$'s configuration for genre $g$.

Figures~\ref{fig:config-own-d12} and \ref{fig:config-own-d34} show these positions for the same 91 cells as the main text. Within a panel, differences between genres come from each genre's standard coordinates and yes rates, not from who holds the configuration. The figures therefore map the genre-by-aspect geometry. They describe a genre's own contribution to a configuration and do not show where the people who hold it sit. Across the 160 genre-configuration cells, the own contributions and the barycenters correlate at 0.84 to 0.95 on each dimension, so the two versions order the cells similarly. The barycenters spread more widely, because the other genres add most of the variation between cells (Section~\ref{sec:config-cloud}).
